en: Since that *bodhicitta* does not become manifest without cultivation (*bhāvanā*), he begins to explain in detail what was briefly set forth immediately prior, starting with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth. Cultivation is the repeated mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward *bodhicitta* itself; for desired accomplishment is certainly not achieved by merely stretching out one's legs. Therefore, one should apply oneself to practice preceded by the formal undertaking of the Vajrasattva vows. As it is said in the *Samādhirāja-sūtra*:
"O Youth, for one whose essence is practice, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is not difficult to attain."

Therefore, he says: "For the sake of others," and so forth. Regarding *nirvāṇa* for the Śrāvakas and others: the twentieth production of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*), which is the culmination of excellence and consists of the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*), is stainless because it is free from the stains of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) along with their latent predispositions (*savāsanā*). It is marvelous due to its association with qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and the unique attributes (*āveṇikadharma*). When that [path] exists, there is freedom from decrease and increase; because, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), its intrinsic nature is emptiness, there is neither decrease nor increase of the adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) and their remedies (*pratipakṣa*). However, conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), they certainly do exist.

To explain how one cultivates [this], he says "five," and so forth. One should not transgress nor should one destroy them. "The three vehicles" refers to those established in the three vehicles (*triyāna*). If that is so, what is the purpose of cultivating things that are already understood even by children and women? He says: "Like a plantain tree. This means that because the nature of ultimate reality superimposed by ignorance does not exist, one realizes it as being pithless; however, this is not because of its non-existence even conventionally. Why? Because form and the other aggregates are equal and identical in essence with the *dharmadhātu* through their lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*).
There is no real distinction of characteristics among them; nor are they unequal, because each possesses its own individual differentiation.

For this very reason, since the natures of annihilation and permanence are untenable, there is a negation of the cultivation of emptiness and non-emptiness. From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the very absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) is the intrinsic nature of form and so forth, which exist conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*); thus, it is not logical to abandon the nature of being both empty and non-empty. As Ārya [Nāgārjuna] said in the *Bodhicittavivaraṇa*, verses 67–68:
When reality is being explained in this way, there is no negation of the conventional;
for apart from the conventional, reality is not perceived.
The conventional is said to be emptiness, and emptiness itself is indeed the conventional.
"Because of the rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), just as in the case of 'produced' and 'impermanent'";
"cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to conceptual construction (*kalpanā*),
because the vast web of conceptual proliferation is rooted in the apprehension of existence and non-existence.

"Unchanging" (*nirvikāra*) means being free from all superimpositions (*samāropa*). "Fearless" (*nirāśaṅka*) means being without doubt. For this very reason, he does not long for any other path. And thus, through the arising of merit, he is free from sin. As it is said in the *Bodhicittavivaraṇa* (108):
"The person who would cultivate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) for even a single moment..."
"It is impossible to calculate that his mass of merit is this great. And in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*:
"Just as the fire at the end of an eon, it burns away great sins in an instant.
And so it is said in the *Tathāgatajñānamudrāsūtra*.

Furthermore, those who in the future time will possess the thought of awakening without despondency, who are firm in their commitment and endowed with a resolute intention toward enlightenment—for them, whatever karma they have accumulated that would necessarily result in experience in the miserable realms will, in that future time, be exhausted merely by a headache, or by mental distress alone, or by great physical illness, or by being born into a poor family.

Thus [it is said]: "He is free from the conceptualization of beginning and end, because he is solely established in the reality that is without beginning or end. For he is of the nature of *bodhicitta*. And that is devoid of self (*ātman*), person (*puruṣa*), individual (*pudgala*), and so forth; it is free from the grasped forms of the aggregates (*skandha*) and from any other grasper; and because the principle [of their nature] is the same—namely, that all phenomena have an illusory (*māyā*) nature—it is primordially unarisen, inseparable from emptiness and compassion, and has emptiness as its very essence. As it has been said in the *Guhyasamājatantra*:

"One's own mind is free from all entities, devoid of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and abandoned of the grasped and the grasper; through the equality of the selflessness of phenomena, it is primordially unarisen and has emptiness as its intrinsic nature.
"Like space" means by way of being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). As Āhārya said:
[Bodhicittavivaraṇa 51]

"The stability of the mind that is without support has the characteristic of space; this very cultivation of space is considered the cultivation of emptiness. And thus, by the words beginning with "nor" (*na ca*), he precludes the possibility that a beginner might turn away from the welfare of sentient beings. One should not conceptualize the existence or non-existence of a sentient being, because both existence and non-existence are untenable. By this, the practice (*pratipatti*) is described; for that consists, in brief, of the cultivation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and the application of the means such as generosity (*dāna*) consisting of cultivation.

That bodhicitta, moreover, consists precisely of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*). For it is said: "free from conceptual proliferation" (*niṣprapañca*), and so forth. Wisdom is the realization of the freedom from conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena. What is this freedom from conceptual proliferation? In brief, whatever conceptual construction there may be—such as existence, non-existence, and so on—all that is error, conceptual proliferation; the absence of proliferation is the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*). [Objection: Is emptiness itself then conceptual proliferation? [Response: No; by the word "emptiness," nothing at all is being affirmed.

For the manifestation of the expression of emptiness illuminates the nature of reality within the mental continuum of those to be trained by demonstrating the exclusion of all superimpositions; thus, that [reality] is figuratively called the "referent" of words such as "emptiness," because there is a definitive determination (*adhyavasāya*) of reality—which consists in the cessation of all superimpositions—arising from those words. The means (*upāya*) is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

"Benefiting sentient beings" (*sattvārthakaraṇa*) means that by means of this [wisdom], the welfare of beings is accomplished. Even in the state of non-conceptuality, because the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) from the cultivation of great compassion are awakened, the performance of the welfare of others proceeds effortlessly. This occurs through great compassion alone, for its existence is due solely to the sovereign power of that [compassion]. For this very reason, the Blessed One is described as being inseparable from emptiness and compassion.

And although that [wisdom] is being cultivated, it is ultimately without an objective support (*nirālambana*), because it arises by taking all phenomena—which are devoid of intrinsic nature—as its object. Therefore, their cultivation occurs through identity alone. However, the distinction between the conventional designations "wisdom" and "means" is produced by way of conceptual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Hence, he says: "become one."

Therefore, he says "no," and so forth, to show that for those who have attained the stage of the simultaneous union (*yuganaddha*), there is no clinging to the meditator, the meditation, and the object of meditation, since liberation arises merely from seeing the non-duality of the two truths. Thus, it is stated that bodhicitta is the body, speech, and mind which transcends the object of meditation, the meditator, and the meditation; which is primordially unarisen, naturally quiescent, and consists of the form of the union of emptiness and compassion. That is the meditation on reality (*tattvabhāvanā*) which occurs precisely through the pacification of all conceptual constructions.

For thus, while it is taught that there is an absence of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding all phenomena which are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), in reality, cultivation—just like the form of an illusion—is not truly cultivation at all, because of their emptiness of intrinsic nature and because they consist of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). However, it is presented merely as a conformity [to conventional understanding]. In this way, an entity such as the form of a deity is not a real object of cultivation, since no cultivation is perceived therein, owing to its nature as conceptual construction. And so it has been said in the *Guhyasamājatantra* (2.3):
"In the absence [of an object], there is an absence of cultivation; cultivation is indeed not cultivation."

Thus, "being" would not be "being," for mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is not perceived. Now, what is the meaning of "non-conceptual cultivation"? The meaning is that cultivation is simply the non-mentation of all phenomena by means of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) as the method. Is it then not faulty to conceptualize great bliss? It is not unfaulty. Because that too is not distinct from the world, it is empty by virtue of the emptiness of the world. Furthermore, since it is impossible to conceptualize that which is empty, the conceptualization of even that is faulty. Nevertheless, it is taught because it is conducive to the non-conceptual. As it has been said in the *Ālokamālā* (15cd):
"Even delusions are beneficial because they eliminate other delusions.

Therefore, the thorough knowledge of all phenomena as being free from conceptual construction is designated as "cultivation" (bhāvanā) in its ultimate sense during the course of the [spiritual] continuum.

If this were so, there would be no conceptual construction such as: "I am now the performer of the two accumulations and shall enjoy their fruits," or "I am the practitioner, the path is that which is to be offered, the two obscurations are what is to be abandoned, and Buddhahood is what is to be attained. And if that were the case, there would be no engagement in or withdrawal from anything whatsoever. This is true; for...
In the investigation of ultimate reality,
there is neither engagement nor withdrawal.

Thus he says: "And not," and so forth. Prior to the time of the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*), engagement and withdrawal indeed exist from the perspective of conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*). This is because one thinks, "This destruction of my defects will come to pass," and thus the engagement in the practice of the path proceeds unimpeded. However, because the certainty regarding reality has not yet become second nature (*sātmībhāva*), the mind remains under the sway of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless ignorance; consequently, only that conventional activity which is inconsistent with such certainty continues to operate. For this very reason, even when the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) has been attained, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is still required.

Regarding how the world is perceived within this very meditation, he says: "Like a city of Gandharvas," and so forth. The meaning is that just as cities of Gandharvas and the like are cognized by the consciousnesses of all the sense faculties conventionally, yet are not apprehended ultimately because they lack intrinsic nature, so too is the world. The connection is with the phrase "some state of existence" (*kācit sthitiḥ*); the remainder of the sentence is "the world is thus."

And since that bodhicitta, consisting of bliss, does not arise without a means (upāya), he indicates the means with the words "Just as," and so forth. Because she has not experienced the pleasure of touch, [she is called] a "maiden" (kumāra) up until the age of eighteen; likewise, a "maiden" (kumārī) is one who is eighteen years old.

This is because it is so stated in the *Vinaya*. Just as some kind of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) arises when those two [the male and female organs] are joined, so too does it arise for the yogin during the meditative union with wisdom (*prajñā*). However, the distinction is that for the arising and the continuous maintenance of great bliss, there must be a meeting of the yogin and wisdom through the practice of the syllable (*akṣara*). He explains this meeting: "having placed the *liṅga* in the *bhaga*. Regarding "the cultivation of the recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānusmṛti-bhāvanā*): the Buddha is the Bodhicitta-Vajra, the Vajradhara; one should cultivate oneself and the wisdom as having that very nature.
However, for one who practices the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), that [wisdom] takes the form of Vajragarvā according to the sequence to be explained;

the sense is that "some wisdom" refers to great bliss (*mahāsukha*). It is "stainless in the beginning, middle, and end," meaning it is non-conceptual at the beginning, middle, and end, because those very characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing do not exist in reality. Alternatively, it is the innate (*sahaja*) and non-conceptual state proximate to the joys of *ānanda*, *paramānanda*, and *viramānanda*.

Thus, he says "for those who see," and so forth, to show that yoga is accomplished even during the state of non-concentration through the cultivation of the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). "Not for those whose minds are directed elsewhere" means for those whose minds are undistracted because they are focused exclusively on reality (*tattva*).

"Unceasingly" means without interruption. For those who have conviction that the world consists solely of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), even when there is no meditative composure due to the activity of conceptual construction, "uncomposed yoga" arises. However, the mind established in reality is non-conceptual; this is "composed yoga. But everything that is turned away from reality is merely distracted. "This" refers to great bliss. It becomes supreme and supramundane through cultivation.

"Consisting of all the perfections" means that giving and the other perfections have that [Mahāmudrā] as their intrinsic nature. By this, its character as the stages beginning with Pramuditā is described. "Supreme cultivation" is said in relation to the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).

Having thus established the nature of cause and effect as well as its pervasiveness, he further consolidates the meditative cultivation with the words "That very... and so forth. "That very" refers to great bliss (*mahāsukha*). "Existence" (*bhāva*) is being; "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is non-being; and neither of these is anything at all. This is because the mind, being devoid of a nature that is either one or many, lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). Alternatively, "existence" (*bhāva*) is defined as that which comes into being (*bhavati*), which is simply a manifestation preceded by non-existence; yet, since there is ultimately no arising, it is of the nature of non-existence. Thus, existence is [ultimately] non-existence.

For this very reason, there is not even the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpatā*) in the form of its cessation (*pracyuti*). As for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) is established, we have set that forth in detail in the *Madhyamakamañjarī* and the *Munimatālaṃkāra* in accordance with scripture; however, in brief, it is presented in the *Abhayapaddhati*.

R Abhayapaddhati (Chapter 13): Therefore, because it has the nature of both existence and non-existence, there is the absence of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Since these [phenomena] have existence and non-existence as their substratum and are pervaded by them, when the pervader is absent, the pervaded is also absent. This alone is the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*): that for one who examines with the eye of wisdom, when the light of correct knowledge arises, there is the non-perception of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). Consequently, yogins of reality, even while established in all modes of conduct and seeing all phenomena, do not see them.

Such non-perception alone is intended, and not that which results from a lack of mental attention, as in the case of one who is asleep or whose eyes are closed. For it is certain that attachment to form and so forth must be removed precisely by the disappearance of the seeds of doubt, and not by being extracted like a thorn. Thus, by setting aside mental engagement with existence, non-existence, intrinsic nature, extrinsic nature, and so on, and having withdrawn the mind from everything, one should not think of anything at all.
Thus it has been said:
"When neither existence nor non-existence stands before the mind," *Bodhicaryāvatāra* 9.35.
Then, due to the absence of any other alternative, she becomes tranquil as she is without objective support (*nirālambā*).

For that yogin who does not think in such a way, there arises the Blessed Lady Prajñā, attained through the grace of the Guru. She is characterized by the cessation of the distinction between the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and their results; her nature is conventionally self-luminous; and because she is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), she is devoid of the flood of suffering that is the nature of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), which consists of conceptual proliferation, and her essential form is supreme bliss. Having directly realized her through the yoga of non-seeing, by the power of that realization, he thinks: "Oh, how great is the power of delusion (*moha*), by which these sentient beings [do not realize] even the nature of nirvāṇa!"

Thinking, "How indeed might I cause them to realize this? and reflecting thus, one takes as one's object the entire world which is of that very nature; then, the non-referential great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) arises. Having arisen, one should perceive oneself as being of that very nature—the form of the arisen maṇḍala, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, consisting of great compassion, and possessing an indivisible nature with the Blessed Lady’s Wisdom (*prajñā*), whose other name is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), because they are of one essence. At that time, there is the identity (*tādātmya*) of emptiness and compassion.

And that is non-conceptual yoga (*nirvikalpa-yoga*). In that regard, whenever stability of the mind occurs, at that very moment there is the yoga of meditative absorption (*samāhita-yoga*); at other times, however, it is simply the yoga of non-absorption (*asamāhita-yoga*). For this very reason, in the stage of the Arisen (*utpanna-krama*), the yoga of meditative absorption is taught even without the yoga of the *mudrā*, because one abides through the means of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) by way of non-conceptualization regarding all phenomena. But the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā-siddhi*) arises only from the yoga of the *mudrā*.
And this indeed is the yoga of the identity (*tādātmya*) of emptiness and compassion. [The stages are:
withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), as well as meditation (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and retention (*dhāraṇā*).
Mindfulness and meditative concentration—this is held to be the six-limbed yoga.
This is the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) as taught in the *Samājottara* (the *Guhyasamājatantra*, 18.141).

For instance, withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is the non-attachment of the sense faculties to their respective objects due to their being of a single flavor with emptiness, like the seeing of a reflection by a maiden; it is so called because it involves the "withdrawing" (*āharaṇa*), that is, the drawing back (*ākarṣaṇa*), of each of those [faculties] from them.

Then, through the departure of distraction, there is meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). That consists of *vitarka*, which is the investigation of the entity, and *vicāra*, which is the analytical examination of the nature of that entity as being emptiness. Thus, by turning away from external objects, one who—through the mind alone and with an inward-turned focus—takes as his object the self whose nature is the deity, and who contemplates it as the single flavor of unsurpassed wisdom and means, experiences a state of mental well-being due to the orientation toward entering reality; this is *prīti* (joy). From that follows *sukha* (bliss), such as the pliancy of the body and so forth.
For one who practices in this way, there is fivefold one-pointedness of mind consisting of wisdom, which culminates exclusively in the emptiness of all phenomena.

Thereafter, *prāṇāyāma* is the activity of the subtle vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*), characterized by its entry, abiding, and emergence solely through the *avadhūtī* path once the *lalanā* and *rasanā* have been obstructed. Then, *dhāraṇā* is the settling of the vital wind—the vehicle of the mind—into the drop of bodhicitta, due to the non-emergence [of the wind] from the *avadhūtī* and the gradual accumulation of earth, water, fire, and air within the pericarp-lotuses of the navel, heart, throat, and forehead, resulting in a single flavor with emptiness.

And at that time, the Caṇḍālī blazes by her very nature; and the moon, ignited by her, flows exceedingly. Then, the bodhicitta within the vajra-jewel—immovable and filled with bliss through the stages of *niṣyanda* and so forth—will gradually attain purity.

Then, when the mind has entered into *dhāraṇā*, there arises—preceded by the appearance of signs (*nimitta*) such as a mirage, smoke, fireflies, a lamp, and constant light—the vision of the deities of the maṇḍala that has arisen, which takes the form of a reflection and is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). Following that comes the radiation of manifold rays of light, and then the radiation of the wheel of deities throughout the three realms; this is *anusmṛti*. For one established therein, an appearance occurs for others as well, according to their respective capacities.
Therefore, that very non-conceptual yoga is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) whose nature is the Great Vajradhara—the body of gnosis consisting of the union of the imperishable great bliss.
As for the benefits of the six limbs, they are stated in the *Samājottara*:
*Q/R Samājottara / Guhyasamājatantra (18.155–157)* [followed by the verses].
Having attained withdrawal (pratyāhāra), one is empowered by all mantras;
having attained the knowledge of meditative concentration (dhyānajñāna), one shall obtain the five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā).
By means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), the Bodhisattvas constantly observe with restraint;
through the power of mental retention (dhāraṇā), Vajrasattva shall always enter [them].
Through the union of recollection, a circle of light is born;
by the mere mastery of meditative concentration, one becomes free from obscurations.
Thus it is said. This very same samādhi was taught by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna in the *Pañcakrama* (5.24–28):
"Fully awakened through the Māyājāla, having crossed to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra..."
The great yogi has accomplished what was to be done and stands firm in the method of the two truths.
This very non-dual gnosis is non-abiding nirvana;
it is likewise buddhahood, the state of a Vajradhara, and all-encompassing sovereignty.
The vajra-like samādhi and the stage of completion (niṣpannakrama),
as well as the illusion-like samādhi— that is called non-duality.
Terms such as "non-arising" and so forth indicate non-dual gnosis;
they are all designations for this very [gnosis], and nothing else is expressed therein.

"The Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have attained through this very [path] the accomplishment whose nature is Mahāmudrā, which is free from the conceptualization of existence and non-existence.
Thus he concludes the section on meditative cultivation with the words beginning "bhāva" (cultivation), etc.

The "faults" (*doṣa*) are those previously mentioned, such as laziness and so forth. The three types of defilements (*saṃkleśa*) are afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and birth. To demonstrate that turning away from these defilements is not difficult, he says: "Not slight," and so forth. All conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are indeed the "darknesses," which are the obscurations to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). "Fickle" refers to a lack of delight in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Passion and the like are the obscurations of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*). "Smearing" (*pralepa*) refers to latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).

It is not an object of apprehension because its very nature is non-existent; for this very reason, it is not an apprehender either, since anything other than that [mind] also lacks the nature of an object of apprehension. That very mind is the supreme *nirvāṇa*, the non-abiding *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, in relation to that mind, there is the state of being the antidote to the rivalry of the "sides" (*kakṣā*). Having investigated—by means of [showing it to be] devoid of a nature that is either one or many—one should make the nature of that mind its own nature, which is the absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*); that is, its innate form. In the reading *abhāvaḥ*, the meaning is: "one should make the non-existence of the mind, which is the absence of intrinsic nature, its own nature."

The connection is: "by that darkness of conceptualization, there shall be bliss. The intended meaning (*tātparya*) lies in the cultivation of the *bodhicitta*. Those who have gone far away from sins are the noble ones (*ārya*). "That" refers to the eon (*kalpa*); "that" refers to bliss. The primary and secondary commitments (*samaya*) and the yoga of the seals (*mudrā*) authorized by the gurus will be explained. Thus, he prohibits [the practitioner] from engaging in other activities for one who cultivates the stage of uninterrupted arising, on the grounds that such activity leads only to distraction. By the words beginning with "what," [he means] the mantra starting with the syllable *oṃ*.

The "image-ego" (*pratimāhaṃkāra*) is the ego-identification with the deity of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*). "Samaya" refers to the five nectars and so forth. By this [statement], it is said that one should not perform even such activities of body, speech, and mind, let alone others; however, the practice of the samayas as they happen to be encountered is permitted provided there is no attachment. If one asks, "What then should he do?", [the author] says: "The target," and so forth. One's own chosen deity is great bliss (*mahāsukha*). As it is said in the *Dvikalpa* [Hevajratantra I.viii]:
"Bodhicitta is the deity" means it should be meditated upon for the sake of generating that which is characterized by union with it. "Like space" means having the single flavor of reality (*tattva*).
"The place" refers to the bodhicitta. "The lotus garden" refers to the charnel ground. The connection is made by changing the case ending: "the desired location."

*Mantra* means "knowledge of the mind" (*mana-jñāna*), or "awakening of the mind" (*mana-avabodhana*), according to the list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*). Furthermore, because it is the primary object of firm conviction, the mantra is precisely the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*) in the form of the non-dual Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) as previously described. Alternatively, since one attains the state of Vajradhara through the abandonment of the two obscurations by means of meditating on such knowledge, that very [knowledge] is the mantra in the sense of being a protection for the mind (*manas-trāṇa*). As will be stated later with reference to the knowledge of the Great Seal: "Therefore..."
By the passage beginning with "that very own mind," and as it is stated in the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tantra* (the *Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhi*).

Furthermore, Lord of Guhyakas, the characteristic of mantras has not been created by all the Buddhas, nor caused to be created, nor approved. Why is that? For this is the very nature of phenomena (dharmatā): whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this nature of phenomena remains constant—namely, the mantra-nature of mantras.

To the extent that when the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, arise in the world, they then—by means of various methods, various intentions, for various dispositions, with various words, various syllables, various explanations and utterances of different lands, and through various tones and cadences—empower and teach the mantra-words. "Explanation" (*nirukti*) refers to the languages of the gods and so forth. Thus, by virtue of his knowledge of mantras, it is indicated that the very knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*) will provide him with supreme protection; what need is there to mention the recitation of conventional protective mantras, as in the case of one who practices [the deity] through the generation stage (*utpattibhāvanā*)? As it is said in the *Bhagavatī*:
“O Kauśika, the Perfection of Wisdom itself will provide him with protection, defense, and guardianship; what need is there for you?

Thus he explains what was indicated by the word “youth” (kumāra), beginning with “by means of wisdom and skillful means” (*prajñopāyena*). “Directly” (*sākṣāt*) means that for a man, there is no wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*), nor is there for a woman a skillful means consisting of cultivation. Therefore, the connection is that one does not attain Buddhahood by directly abandoning external wisdom (*bāhyaprajñā*). [She is] divine and captivating, because this cultivation-based wisdom is indeed one and the same.

Without the single external wisdom (*bāhyaprajñā*) conjoined with a consort—that is, without the accomplishment sealed by an external consort—the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā is not granted; for it is precisely from the meditative union (*samāpatti*) with an external consort that the gnosis of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) arises. For this very reason, the yoga with an external consort is said to be the direct means (*sākṣādupāya*) for the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā.

However, even in the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), both the woman and the man should resolve that their own self is the form of the deity as it has arisen; thus, the intention of one who says "each one" is that there would be wisdom (*prajñā*) consisting of both. In the stage of generation, however, there may be even a single *jñānamudrā*; yet at the time of accomplishment (*siddhi*), even that consists of both. Therefore, the four seals (*caturmudrā*) are to be applied in both stages. Among them, in the stage of generation, the external wisdom is the *karmamudrā*, because she bestows joy (*mudaṃ rāti*) through acts such as embracing.

Internal wisdom (*adhyātmaprajñā*) is *avadhūtī*, whose nature is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) of a single flavor with emptiness; it is the *dharmadhātu* and the *dharmamudrā*. The unsurpassed *bodhicitta*, consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), is the fruit-form *mahāmudrā*. The emanation of various deities is the *samayamudrā*. Alternatively, that very [wisdom] is the *karmamudrā*; when established by the culmination of the purification of that same aforementioned *mahāmudrā*, it is the *dharmamudrā*, because its intrinsic nature is the *dharmakāya*, which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the mind.

The *sambhogakāya*, which is embraced by the *karmamudrā* and adorned with the primary and secondary marks according to its appropriate form, and the *nirmāṇakāya*, which takes the form of infinite and diverse mandala circles and so forth, is the *samayamudrā* because it does not fail at the time of benefiting those disciples who are worthy of training. Bodhicitta, however, is the body of great bliss (*mahāsukhakāya*) and the *svābhāvikakāya* because its nature is emptiness; and it is the *mahāmudrā* because of its all-pervasiveness.

Mudrā is the sealing of phenomena, which is their very nature; primarily, this is *bodhicitta* itself because other mudrās possess that same nature, and thus they are indeed "mudrās" [in the sense of being seals]. Alternatively, a mudrā is that which bestows great joy (*mudaṃ rāti*), namely the *saṃbhogakāya*, whose form is endowed with signs such as hands, faces, and the brilliance of the primary and secondary marks. The *samayamudrā* is the *dharmakāya*, the nature of the mind, to be realized within oneself; for it is said that "samaya" means perfect awakening (*sambodha*).

The *dharmamudrā* consists of speech that reveals the reality (*tattva*) of phenomena in their various forms, as it is the basis for the *dharmasambhogakāya*. The *karmamudrā* is the *nirmāṇakāya*, because it accomplishes activities through various emanations due to its nature of performing deeds. Alternatively, the *karmamudrā* is the *nirmāṇakāya*, the *dharmamudrā* is the *dharmakāya*, and the *mahāmudrā* is the *sambhogakāya*. The *samayamudrā* is the *bodhicitta*, because it is the form of the union of great bliss, emptiness, compassion, and all phenomena.

The "meeting" (*milana*) of form and the other [sensory objects] occurs because they are perceived through their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) has been established in this manner within the commentary on the phrase "consisting of this" (*evam-maya*). Furthermore, these four seals (*mudrā*) should be understood by the wise as each being composed of four seals; however, they are not explicitly stated here for fear of excessive prolixity.

In the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), the action seal (*karmamudrā*) is precisely the external wisdom (*prajñā*) who has been meditated upon in the form of the chosen goddess. The knowledge seal (*jñānamudrā*), which is another name for one's own consort, as well as the *hūṃ* syllable and so forth meditated within the body, is the dharma seal (*dharmamudrā*). The commitment seal (*samayamudrā*), however, is that which is produced from seed-syllables and so forth; it also refers to the deities gathered in the mandala circle who perform the emanation and reabsorption [of light], as well as their hand symbols (*cihna*). The great seal (*mahāmudrā*) is the very form of oneself as the central deity; therefore, the circle of emanating deities is also the commitment seal.

All these systematic presentations were established by the Blessed One himself in other tantras in accordance with the diverse dispositions of those to be trained; however, the specific texts have not been cited here for fear of prolixity.

Here, however, he establishes [the matter] otherwise with the words beginning "delusion" (*moha*), etc. (237v/478). "Passion" (*rāga*) refers to pure passion, namely Amitābha and Ratnasambhava; for that has as its intrinsic nature the mind (*manas*) which experiences pure pleasure. For in the impure state, feeling (*vedanā*) itself has the nature of the mind, because—as was stated previously—in the experience of pleasant feelings and so forth, there arises the conceit (*asmimāna*) such as "I am happy. "Knowledge" (*vidyā*) is external. Therein, in the vessel, is the form of the deity belonging to both knowledge and means, whether by way of the completion stage (*utpannakrama*) or the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).

And the cultivation of the forms of the deities will be explained. (238r/479) [The word] "from delusion" (*mohāt*) is a fifth-case ablative used with the elision of the suffix *-lyap*. Vairocana is "peaceful. His peacefulness arises because, through investigation, there is the realization that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); this is due to his having the nature of delusion—which consists in such realization—and because he is established in the samādhi of peace. Akṣobhya and Amoghasiddhi are "wrathful" because they manifest externally in the form of wrath solely through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Wrath is a mental agitation directed toward sentient beings or non-sentient objects.

In this context, however, hatred (*dveṣa*) and envy (*īrṣyā*) are called "anger" (*krodha*), because envy is the cause of anger. Amitābha and Ratnasaṃbhava are [the manifestations of] passion (*rakta*). Here, passion refers to both passion (*rāga*) and pride (*māna*). The meaning is that, having observed the delusion (*moha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), passion (*rāga*), and pride (*māna*) of others, he performs the respective acts of purification for each. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of that purpose" (*tadarthaprakaraṇam*): that purpose (*artha*) consists in the nature of those various purifications; "for the sake of that" means for the sake of performing that excellent activity (*prakṛṣṭaṃ karaṇam*). The Victor Vajradhara is endowed with these forms of Vairocana and the others.

Regarding the specific time for one who has not attained mastery and is unable to practice the mudrā without interruption day and night, he says "at dawn," and so forth. "Properly" means without distraction. Just as an intense innate experience (sahajānubhava) implants a latent impression (*vāsanā*) of mindfulness, otherwise, because the experience is weak, there will be no accomplishment at all for one who fails to remember it or who does not practice uninterrupted great bliss. "Only one's own mind" refers precisely to the *bodhicitta*.

"Of her" means having resolved with conviction upon the innate bliss (*sahajasukha*)—whether it has been experienced during the ritual sprinkling (*seka*) or at another time—as being present within the mind. It is with reference to this very [bliss] that the "hand-seal" (*karamudrā*) is taught elsewhere. The connection is: "one should practice the yoga" together with an external consort (*mudrā*). In this context, one who is skilled and proficient in yoga [is meant]. "Even from among animals" implies that one should bring a female animal (*tiraścīm*). Thus it is said in the *Vajrārallitantra*: "Then he spoke of the Vajra-worship..."
In a secluded and solitary place, or within the inner chambers of one's own home,
one should worship a twelve-year-old girl, as well as a sixteen-year-old,
a twenty-five-year-old maiden, a cow, and likewise a buffalo.

One whose self is Heruka should indeed desire a female monkey, a female dog, a female donkey, a female camel, a female deer, a female goat, a female pig, or one born of a gava-ya; he will certainly attain accomplishment, there is no doubt.

"Directly" means with an external *mudrā*, and not with a *jñānamudrā* alone. Beyond one year, the commitment (*samaya*)—the union with the *mudrā*—is not to be transgressed. Negligence regarding that is a "transgression. From the yoga, which is great bliss; the restoration of the commitment is by means of the consecration of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*). In particular, when the commitment is damaged, the bodhicitta, which is the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion, must be recollected. One who possesses the yoga of Amoghasiddhi, however, may be "weak" [in this regard] and should receive all the consecrations. "Perform"—he should perform it.

The restraint (*saṃvara*) has been stated and will be further explained. However, the unsurpassed restraint is the *bodhicitta*, because it is the condensed form of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). This is because the *bodhicitta* restrains one from all unwholesome states and from false conceptualizations (*asatkalpanā*). The secret substances (*rahasyadravya*), which will be described later, are for the sake of increasing enthusiasm throughout the year. Regarding the phrase "by means of mantra and tantra": this refers to the visualizations (*dhyāna*)—namely, the explanations of the mantras that will be described—which are performed by the practitioner of the generation stage (*utpattiyogin*) for the purpose of [realizing] the five-family clusters (*pañcakulakalāpinī*) and so forth.

He concludes with "In this way," and so forth. "The three worlds" refers to heaven, the mortal realm, and the netherworld (*pātāla*). Among these, heaven extends from the abodes of the Mahārājikas up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Alternatively, the three worlds are the three realms beginning with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), or they are body, speech, and mind; one should meditate upon them as having the nature of the bodhicitta consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
The sixth cluster in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*.
